articles.title: The GCC & Southeast Asia Skills Ledger 2026: where capability gaps are widening
articles.subtitle: Demand for digital, analytical and leadership skills is outrunning supply in both regions. Our analysis shows where the gap is largest — and which employers are closing it fastest.
articles.author: arif-santoso
keyTakeaways: Across both regions, demand for advanced digital and data skills is growing roughly twice as fast as the talent pool able to meet it.
Leadership capability, not technical skill, is the most-cited bottleneck to transformation among the executives we interviewed.
Employers that pair skills data with internal mobility fill critical roles up to 40 percent faster than those relying on external hiring.
The organisations closing the gap fastest treat reskilling as a capital investment with a board-level owner and a measurable return.

carouselItems.caption: Capability academies are moving out of HR and into the business: most new programmes in our sample are co-owned by an operating executive.

carouselItems.quote: We stopped asking how many people we trained. We now ask how many critical roles we can fill from inside within ninety days.

Skills-based talent marketplaces surface hidden capability: in one bank, 1 in 5 data roles was filled by an employee from a non-technical function.

paragraphs: For most of the past decade, the conversation about skills in the Gulf and Southeast Asia has been framed as a pipeline problem: produce more graduates in the right disciplines and the gap will close. Our latest research suggests that framing is no longer adequate. The gap is widening not because the pipeline has stalled, but because the skills that matter are changing faster than any pipeline can adapt.

Drawing on assessment data, job-posting analysis and interviews with more than forty senior executives, the Skills Ledger 2026 maps where demand is outrunning supply — and identifies the employers that are closing the gap fastest. The pattern is consistent across both regions: organisations that treat capability as a strategic asset, measured and managed like any other, are pulling away from those that treat it as a training budget.

contentSections.heading: Demand is compounding faster than supply
paragraphs: Across the five capability clusters we track, demand has grown far faster than the pool of people able to meet it. The gap is widest in AI and data, where demand has nearly doubled since 2023 while available talent has grown by roughly a fifth. Cloud, cybersecurity and green skills show a similar shape.

Customer-facing skills are the exception. Here supply has broadly kept pace, largely because employers have invested heavily in service academies over the past five years. That experience is instructive: where organisations commit to building a capability at scale, the gap can be closed within a planning cycle.

contentSections.heading: Leadership is the binding constraint
paragraphs: When we asked executives to name the single capability gap that most limits their transformation agenda, technical skills came second. Leadership and change capability came first — cited by a third of respondents. Leaders who can translate strategy into new ways of working, and bring sceptical teams with them, are in shorter supply than data scientists.
This matters because leadership gaps compound technical ones. A data team without a leader who can connect its work to the business produces dashboards, not decisions.

pullQuote.text: We can hire data scientists. What we cannot hire fast enough are leaders who know what to ask them.
pullQuote.author: Ratna Wijaya
pullQuote.title: Chief Learning Officer, Nusantara Digital Bank

contentSections.heading: Investment is rising — and diverging
paragraphs: Reskilling investment per employee in our GCC sample overtook the global benchmark in 2022 and has continued to accelerate. National programmes and large employers alike have made capability a stated priority, and budgets have followed.

Spending alone, however, does not predict outcomes. The organisations in our sample with the highest returns spend more on fewer, deeper programmes that are tied to specific roles — and they measure results in business terms rather than course completions.

contentSections.heading: Inside the organisations closing the gap
paragraphs: Three practices separate the fastest movers. First, they build a live picture of skills across the workforce, rather than relying on job titles. Second, they use that picture to move people internally before hiring externally. Third, they give a senior business leader — not only HR — accountability for capability outcomes.

The effect on time to fill critical roles is striking. Organisations combining internal mobility with skills data fill those roles in a little over five weeks on average, against more than three months for international hiring.

contentSections.heading: An agenda for the next eighteen months
paragraphs: For executive teams, the implication is that capability needs the same discipline as capital. That means a clear inventory of the skills the strategy requires, an owner for each critical gap, and a quarterly review of progress that sits alongside financial performance.

It also means accepting that the half-life of skills is shortening. The goal is not to close the gap once but to build an organisation that can keep closing it — one that learns as fast as its market changes.

pullQuote.text: The question is no longer whether you have the skills you need. It is whether you can build them faster than they expire.
pullQuote.author: Sofia Marquez
pullQuote.title: Labour Economist, Meridian Policy Institute

articles.title: AI copilots and the new shape of the frontline workday
articles.subtitle: Generative assistants are reaching branch staff, technicians and call-centre agents. Early pilots show the biggest gains go to the least experienced workers.
articles.author: arif-santoso
keyTakeaways: Frontline AI pilots in our sample cut time spent searching for information by roughly a third.
Productivity gains were largest for new joiners, narrowing the gap with experienced colleagues.
Adoption depended more on supervisor coaching than on the quality of the tool itself.

charts.title: Productivity uplift after six months of AI copilot use
charts.subtitle: Percentage change in tasks completed per shift, by tenure
charts.source: Birds Research Desk analysis. Illustrative data for demonstration.

paragraphs: The first wave of generative AI adoption was concentrated in knowledge work: marketing, software development, analysis. The second wave is reaching the frontline — the branch officer, the field technician, the warehouse supervisor and the contact-centre agent. These roles make up the majority of employment in both the GCC and Southeast Asia, and the stakes are correspondingly larger.
Pilots we reviewed across logistics, banking and utilities point to a consistent pattern: the assistant acts less like an automation engine and more like an always-available senior colleague.

contentSections.heading: The great leveller
paragraphs: The most striking finding is who benefits. Workers in their first six months saw productivity gains several times larger than veterans. The copilot effectively packages the tacit knowledge of experienced staff and makes it available on demand.

pullQuote.text: Our newest dispatchers now perform like people with two years on the job. That changes how we think about hiring and onboarding.
pullQuote.author: Aditya Rao
pullQuote.title: VP, People Analytics, Straits Logistics Group

contentSections.heading: Supervisors make or break adoption
paragraphs: Usage rates varied widely between teams using the same tool. The difference was the supervisor: teams whose leaders modelled the tool, shared prompts and reviewed outputs together reached high adoption within weeks. Teams left to self-serve often stalled.
For executives, the lesson is that frontline AI is a leadership programme as much as a technology rollout.

articles.title: What chief learning officers learned from three years of capability academies
articles.subtitle: Academies promised to turn learning into a strategic engine. Five CLOs share what worked, what did not, and what they would do differently.
articles.author: layla-haddad
keyTakeaways: Academies anchored to a business outcome outlived those anchored to a catalogue of courses.
Faculty drawn from inside the business raised credibility and application rates.
The hardest part was not design but sustaining sponsorship after the launch year.

carouselItems.caption: Cohort learning labs replaced lecture halls in most of the academies we visited.

carouselItems.quote: The day we let line managers co-teach, attendance stopped being a problem.
carouselItems.caption: Kenji Watanabe, Head of Leadership Development, Pacific Rim Manufacturing
Capstone projects tied to live business problems became the academies’ calling card.

paragraphs: Three years ago, the capability academy became the signature move of ambitious learning functions. Rather than a catalogue of courses, an academy would build a specific capability — data literacy, customer centricity, operational excellence — at scale, with a clear link to strategy.
We asked five chief learning officers who launched academies in that period to look back honestly.

contentSections.heading: Start with the business problem
paragraphs: Every CLO we spoke with agreed that the academies that survived were those launched to solve a named business problem. An academy built to support a digital banking launch had a clear purpose and a natural sponsor. One built to "improve leadership" drifted.

pullQuote.text: An academy without a business owner is just a nicer course catalogue.
pullQuote.author: Ratna Wijaya
pullQuote.title: Chief Learning Officer, Nusantara Digital Bank

contentSections.heading: Teach from the inside
paragraphs: Using internal practitioners as faculty, supported by external experts, consistently raised both credibility and application. Participants trusted colleagues who had faced the same constraints.

contentSections.heading: Sustaining momentum
paragraphs: The most common regret was underestimating year two. Launch energy fades, sponsors move on and budgets are re-examined. The academies that endured had built measurement in from day one, so they could show progress when it mattered.

articles.title: Compassion as an operating system: leading teams through restructuring
articles.subtitle: Restructuring erodes trust quickly. Leaders who pair candour with care recover engagement in months rather than years.
articles.author: noor-al-rashid
keyTakeaways: Engagement typically drops sharply after a restructuring announcement; how leaders communicate determines the depth and length of the dip.
Teams led with high candour and high care recovered to baseline engagement in roughly two quarters.
Compassion is a set of observable behaviours that can be taught, not a personality trait.

charts.title: Team engagement after a restructuring announcement
charts.subtitle: Engagement index, baseline = 100
charts.source: Birds Research Desk analysis. Illustrative data for demonstration.

paragraphs: Few moments test a leader like a restructuring. Decisions are made under pressure, information is incomplete, and every message is read for what it does not say. In that environment, the instinct of many executives is to retreat into process.
Our research suggests the opposite instinct pays off. Leaders who combine radical candour about what is changing with visible care for the people affected protect both trust and performance.

contentSections.heading: The engagement dip is inevitable; its depth is not
paragraphs: Every team in our sample experienced a fall in engagement after the announcement. But teams whose leaders scored high on both candour and care recovered to their baseline within about two quarters, while others remained well below it a year later.

contentSections.heading: What compassionate leaders actually do
paragraphs: Compassion in this context is practical. It means telling people what you know and what you do not, as early as you can. It means holding conversations in person, giving people time to react, and following through on every commitment — however small.
It also means caring for those who stay. Survivors of restructuring often carry guilt and anxiety that, left unaddressed, shows up as attrition six months later.

pullQuote.text: People forgive hard decisions. They do not forgive being kept in the dark.
pullQuote.author: Dr. Fatima Siddiqui
pullQuote.title: Organisational Psychologist, Oasis Wellbeing Partners

contentSections.heading: Building the capability
paragraphs: The leaders who handled restructuring well were rarely naturals. Most had been prepared through scenario practice, peer coaching and clear guidance on the conversations they would need to hold. That preparation is a modest investment relative to the cost of lost trust.

articles.title: From Riyadh to Jakarta: five L&D models worth borrowing
articles.subtitle: A photo essay on the learning systems that are quietly redefining workforce development across two of the world’s fastest-changing regions.
articles.author: layla-haddad
keyTakeaways: National skills strategies are shaping corporate learning priorities more directly than in the past.
Apprenticeship and work-integrated models are gaining ground over classroom programmes.
Mobile-first microlearning is the default in Southeast Asia, not an add-on.

charts.title: How learning hours are delivered in our regional sample
charts.subtitle: Share of total formal learning hours
charts.source: Birds Research Desk analysis. Illustrative data for demonstration.

carouselItems.caption: Riyadh: a national academy model links employer demand directly to accredited training.
Dubai: government and private employers co-design leadership programmes for the public sector.
Singapore: individual learning accounts put reskilling choices in employees’ hands.
Jakarta: digital banks run mobile-first academies reaching thousands of staff in weeks.
Ho Chi Minh City: manufacturers pair apprenticeships with supervisor coaching on the line.

paragraphs: The most interesting innovations in workforce development are not always where commentators look. Across the Gulf and Southeast Asia, employers and governments are experimenting with models that combine national ambition, digital delivery and learning in the flow of work.
We travelled through five cities to document them.

contentSections.heading: Learning has moved closer to the work
paragraphs: Across our sample, the largest share of formal learning hours now takes place on the job or through apprenticeships, with mobile microlearning second. The classroom remains important for leadership development, but it is no longer the default.

contentSections.heading: What travels well
paragraphs: Not every model transfers. National academies depend on policy support; mobile-first academies depend on a digitally fluent workforce. But two principles travel everywhere: design learning around real roles, and measure it by what people can do afterwards.

pullQuote.text: The best programmes we see are designed backwards — from the job people will do on Monday morning.
pullQuote.author: Claire Dubois
pullQuote.title: Partner, Executive Education, Lumen Business School

articles.title: Cognitive load is the hidden tax on transformation
articles.subtitle: Most change programmes add initiatives without removing any. The result is an attention deficit that quietly undermines execution.
articles.author: mei-lin-tan
keyTakeaways: Managers in our sample juggled an average of seven concurrent change initiatives.
Self-reported focus time fell sharply once more than four initiatives were active.
Explicitly retiring old priorities is as important as launching new ones.

charts.title: Focused work time by number of concurrent change initiatives
charts.subtitle: Hours of uninterrupted focus per week, managers
charts.source: Birds Research Desk analysis. Illustrative data for demonstration.

paragraphs: Transformation programmes are usually judged on whether they deliver their intended changes. Rarely do they account for the mental bandwidth those changes consume. Yet attention is finite, and when it runs out, execution suffers in ways that rarely appear in a programme dashboard.

contentSections.heading: The attention cliff
paragraphs: Our survey of managers found a sharp decline in focused work once more than four initiatives were running concurrently. Beyond that point, days fragment into meetings, updates and context switches.

pullQuote.text: Every new initiative feels small on its own. Together they are a second full-time job.
pullQuote.author: Dr. Fatima Siddiqui
pullQuote.title: Organisational Psychologist, Oasis Wellbeing Partners

contentSections.heading: Designing for the mind
paragraphs: Leaders can reduce the tax. Sequence initiatives instead of stacking them. Retire old priorities publicly when new ones begin. Protect blocks of focus time, and measure the cognitive load of a programme alongside its milestones.

articles.title: Measuring learning ROI the board will actually believe
articles.subtitle: Boards are asking harder questions about people investments. Here is a measurement approach that links learning to the metrics directors care about.
articles.author: daniel-ferreira
keyTakeaways: Completion rates and satisfaction scores carry little weight with boards; business-outcome metrics do.
A small number of well-designed control-group comparisons is more persuasive than a large dashboard.
Linking capability metrics to ESG reporting is creating a new audience for learning data.

charts.title: Which learning metrics boards find credible
charts.subtitle: Share of directors rating each metric “highly credible”
charts.source: Birds Research Desk analysis. Illustrative data for demonstration.

charts.title: Sales productivity: programme cohort vs control group
charts.subtitle: Revenue per rep, indexed to month 0 = 100
charts.source: Birds Research Desk analysis. Illustrative data for demonstration.

paragraphs: Learning functions have never had more data, yet many still struggle to answer the board’s simplest question: what did we get for the money? The problem is rarely a lack of measurement. It is measuring the wrong things.

contentSections.heading: Speak the board’s language
paragraphs: Directors we surveyed placed very little weight on completion rates. Metrics tied to revenue, productivity and the ability to fill critical roles internally were far more persuasive.

contentSections.heading: Fewer, better comparisons
paragraphs: The most credible evidence comes from simple comparisons: a cohort that went through a programme against a similar group that did not. One well-run comparison over twelve months will do more for a learning budget than a hundred dashboard tiles.

pullQuote.text: When we showed the board a control group, the conversation moved from cost to investment in a single meeting.
pullQuote.author: Aditya Rao
pullQuote.title: VP, People Analytics, Straits Logistics Group

contentSections.heading: The ESG connection
paragraphs: Human-capital disclosures are becoming part of sustainability reporting. That gives learning leaders a new audience — and a new reason to measure rigorously.

pullQuote.text: Capability is now a governance topic. Investors want to know whether the workforce can deliver the strategy.
pullQuote.author: Omar Khalil
pullQuote.title: Group Head of ESG & Sustainability, Arabian Coast Utilities

articles.title: The competency unlock playbook: twelve capabilities for the 2030 executive
articles.subtitle: A practical framework — with an action table — for turning a leadership competency model into behaviour that shows up every week.
articles.author: noor-al-rashid
keyTakeaways: Most competency models describe what good looks like but not how to practise it.
Twelve capabilities cluster into four domains: sense, decide, mobilise and renew.
Each capability should map to a weekly practice, a stretch assignment and a measure.

charts.title: Executive self-assessment vs 360° rating, by domain
charts.subtitle: Average score out of 5
charts.source: Birds Research Desk analysis. Illustrative data for demonstration.

paragraphs: Most large organisations have a leadership competency model. Few can say it changes how leaders behave on a Tuesday afternoon. The gap is not in the model but in translation: competencies are described as outcomes, not as practices.

contentSections.heading: Four domains, twelve capabilities
paragraphs: Our framework groups twelve capabilities into four domains. Executives consistently rate themselves higher than their colleagues do, with the largest gaps in mobilising others and renewing themselves.

contentSections.heading: The action table
paragraphs: For each capability, we recommend a weekly practice, a stretch assignment and a simple measure. A selection is shown below.

actionTable.caption: Competency unlock action table (selection)
rows: Check in with one peer outside your unit
Share one lesson from a failure
Take on an unfamiliar role for 90 days

pullQuote.text: A competency becomes real when it has a calendar slot.
pullQuote.author: Kenji Watanabe
pullQuote.title: Head of Leadership Development, Pacific Rim Manufacturing

contentSections.heading: Making it stick
paragraphs: The organisations that got results reviewed progress on these practices in regular performance conversations, not in a separate development process. Capability became part of how work was managed rather than an annual exercise.

articles.title: Field notes: running a leadership pilot in ninety days
articles.subtitle: A step-by-step account of how one manufacturer designed, ran and evaluated a leadership pilot for plant managers in three months.
articles.author: mei-lin-tan
keyTakeaways: A narrow scope — one capability, one population — made a ninety-day pilot possible.
Baseline measures captured in week one made the final evaluation credible.
Participants’ managers were briefed before the pilot began, not after.

paragraphs: Pilots are often where good leadership programmes go to die: too small to matter, too long to sustain attention. This one was different. In ninety days, a regional manufacturer designed, delivered and evaluated a programme for thirty plant managers.

contentSections.heading: Weeks 1–3: narrow the problem
paragraphs: The team chose a single capability — coaching frontline supervisors — and a single population. They captured baseline measures of supervisor turnover and safety observations before anything else happened.

contentSections.heading: Weeks 4–10: learn by doing
paragraphs: Plant managers met in small peer groups every two weeks, practised coaching conversations on real cases and committed to one change before the next session.

pullQuote.text: We spent less time in the classroom and more time on the shop floor. That was the point.
pullQuote.author: Kenji Watanabe
pullQuote.title: Head of Leadership Development, Pacific Rim Manufacturing

contentSections.heading: Weeks 11–13: evaluate honestly
paragraphs: The evaluation compared pilot plants with similar plants that had not yet joined. The results were strong enough to justify scale-up — and honest enough to show which elements needed redesign.

articles.title: Decision fatigue in the C-suite, and how the best leaders manage it
articles.subtitle: Senior executives make hundreds of decisions a week. New research on attention suggests how to protect the ones that matter most.
articles.author: mei-lin-tan
keyTakeaways: Decision quality in our sample declined measurably late in long meeting days.
Leaders who pre-committed to decision rules delegated more and reversed fewer decisions.
Scheduling the most consequential decisions early in the day is a simple, effective habit.

charts.title: Where executive decision time goes
charts.subtitle: Share of weekly decision time, by decision type
charts.source: Birds Research Desk analysis. Illustrative data for demonstration.

paragraphs: The modern executive diary is a sequence of decisions, large and small, from approvals and escalations to strategy and people. The cumulative load is easy to underestimate.

contentSections.heading: Small decisions crowd out big ones
paragraphs: Operational approvals consumed the largest share of executives’ decision time in our sample; strategic choices the smallest. Many of those approvals could be delegated with clear rules.

contentSections.heading: Habits that protect judgement
paragraphs: The leaders who managed fatigue best shared three habits: they pre-committed to decision rules, delegated reversible decisions, and placed their most consequential choices early in the day.

pullQuote.text: Judgement is a resource. The best executives spend it deliberately.
pullQuote.author: Claire Dubois
pullQuote.title: Partner, Executive Education, Lumen Business School
